news_communities.title: Erratic driver crashes in Lynn, sent to hospital
news_communities.author: Nicole Garcia
news_communities.summary:
A driver who was reportedly driving erratically in Lynn crashed Sunday and was taken to Massachusetts General Hospital.

Lynn Police said an officer tried to stop the vehicle on Grant Street, but the driver did not stop. The officer did not chase the vehicle.

The vehicle later crashed at an intersection on Chestnut Street. The driver was trapped inside and believed to have sustained moderate to possibly life-threatening injuries.

The driver was sent to MGH where medical staff determined the injuries were not life threatening.

The police have not publicly identified the driver and the investigation remains ongoing. Criminal charges are pending.

news_communities.title: From the archives: Sal Baglio’s Uncanny Masterpiece: Music for Abandoned Amusement Parks is a Tour de Force of Music and Storytelling
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
Review by Frank Conte

Since he began writing songs at the age of 12 in his Paris Street flat in East Boston, Sal Baglio channeled the many places of wonder around him, whether they be the long-gone Central Music shop, where he awaited the latest record release from his musical heroes; or the Sacred Heart school playground where he chased girls around; or Suffolk Downs known to him for the Beatles of 1966 not the thoroughbreds. And, then there was the most magical of places, the amusement park. In his time there were a few — Paragon Park, Pleasure Island and the closest with a Blue Line ride, Revere Beach Boulevard if one could call it that.  

These veritable little discounted Disneys are the subject of Baglio’s recent work: Music for Abandoned Amusement Parks. It is—to borrow a phrase from Pete Townsend — an uncanny masterpiece. *  Indeed, it is that good, so good other artists are sure to envy it. Crafted in uncertain times, MFAAP takes us away from the doldrums of the pandemic with a musical journey into a lost world. But the delightful mysteriousness commands your attention, replay upon replay.

Great works impose themselves upon you. MFAAP is a concept album that must heard as intended by the artist: 16 pieces of varied but short length. Heard in order from start to finish.  It’s not to be heard in bits and pieces in shuffle mode. No, the aesthetic unity of all the pieces draws you in as a story unfolds. Style, technique, balance, harmony and narrative are found here.  

Above all, MFAAP is infused with meaning and a great sense of place delivered with the right touch. It is a pity that such music cannot break through universally.

It is a chapel with the soul of a cathedral. Short instrumentals hover over like the soundtrack of a David Lynch film, moving you along and introducing the next scene. Memories are refreshed and so are themes of joy and sadness. Invitations are announced. The opening song, “Funhouse Mirrors” commands: “Arise, arise today’s the day the carnival arrives/ like the perfect birthday gift unwrapped before our eyes/ hurry, hurry let’s all scurry/ for our favorite rides.” An occasional mellotron punctuates the story, often complementing the harmonics of a perfectly strummed guitar. Carnival sound effects show up at the right time. When necessary, electric guitars blare, then soothe at just the right moments before exploding in cacophony as the story demands. Homages to Baglio’s many influences emerge tactfully and tastefully (as in “Song for an Abandoned Amusement Park” which could well have been written by Lennon and McCartney.) There’s also a swirl of Nashville there (“Candy Apple Girl”) and a bit of New Wave (infused in “Black Mascara”) and a touch of classical guitar (“Addio” and “Ghosts of the Promenade.”)

This is more than just music. It’s storytelling of the kind that an older and wiser Baglio has refined as a solo artist now that he’s retired The Stompers, his legendary Boston rock band.  In the spotlight alone, he does not fail to shine.

Clearly this is not Freddy Cannon’s “Palisades Park” (a Baglio favorite). And, it certainly is not a joy ride all the way through and good times lead to worrisome ones. In Baglio’s reading, amusement parks were all magic domains of first dates, first kisses and first loves. The first half recounts these appropriate passions and all the fun: wild roller coasters, funhouse mirrors, houses of horror, arcades, candy apples and cotton candy.  They hold a special place that animates Baglio’s creative spirit, “a pocket full of memories… that are locked there in a world apart from everything’s that’s seen.”

But amusements parks die and memories drift. Others have stories to tell, Baglio reminds us: the tragic characters that make joy rides run: the carnys whose stories are rarely front and center.  In Baglio’s telling, they are the ones who “try to fit in but just get stuck.”  No quiet lives of desperation have ever been captured so beautifully.  

 “Song for an Abandoned Amusement Park” the most Beatle-esque tune with its great chorus — shifts the tone of the narrative, an almost supernatural pivot.  Slowly moving toward despair, the last carney ghost dances on a wooden leg on the ground where the missing teeth of barkers are buried and where the matterhorn ride is torn down “just before the plague.” Now, “The boys and girls all on the tilt-a-whirl are ghosts/ At the funhouse mirrors/ their shattered slivered hosts.” The joy rides come to a close.

The album’s hardest rocker is “Freaks,” an edgy, defiant cry on behalf of the of the alienated carny. “I never cared for people/They’re brutal and unreal/ I like to stay alone/In my trailer by the Ferris wheel/I work as a carny/With a girl name of peg/She likes to carve her name into my wooden leg.” Delivered with a great guitar energy worthy of Adrian Belew, “Freaks” unveils our carny’s impeding fate as he mocks death marching quickly toward it but apparently just not yet. “When I die don’t bury me/Scatter my ashes neath the dogwood tree/Sing a song and dance around/ And send me off to Gibson town.”

Baglio leads us to “Music for Abandoned Amusement Music Parks No. 2” which lends a whistling-beyond-the-graveyard feel — setting up the album’s climatic piece.  Here we find a master at work.

The artist takes “Freaks” and strips it to its essence revealing its loneliness before the darkness comes. Shorn of its edginess and fabulous noise, “Freaks” is transformed into “Freak,” an elegy for the carney whose last midnight dance has long passed.  On death’s door, the carney is stoic, devoid of any future hope. Baglio’s device here (in one of the album’s longer pieces) is most sublime keeping it all minimal and avoiding the temptation of greater instrumentation that is better used later. His singing of the last altered lines is heartbreaking. “When I die don’t bury me/Drag my ass to that dogwood tree/Salute me with a beer and song/Leave my bones here in Gibson town.” Evocative elegies do not come better than “Freak.” The tears are all too real. 

In the end, it is not only souls who are abandoned but the entire juggernaut. The finale —in the vein of the looping techniques found in the post-performance work of the Beatles (think Revolution 9) — conveys the collapse of the physical world leaving only the ghosts of kids and carneys in the midst. As a coda (and ironically the work’s longest piece) the instrumental “Music for Abandoned Amusement Parks No. 3″ swells early with a symphonic quality before giving way to tin drums and a saturnalia of guitar feedback and sound engineering that carry our ghostly voices back and forth. Tranquility comes at the end, found in the last notes of a lonesome carousel. And so, the apocalypse arrives with its beauty, terror and sheer humanity in a lost world full of distortion that can be beautiful and frightening at the same time. * * 

The term masterpiece is thrown around too recklessly in contemporary culture. It would take some undertaking of a godly pursuit to think of Music for Abandoned Amusement Parks as anything other than a masterpiece.

Frank Conte is the editor and publisher of EastBoston.com

Music for Abandoned Amusement Parks is available on Bandcamp and Apple Music.

*Upon hearing King Crimson’s In the Court of the Crimson King in 1969, an awestruck Pete Townsend of The Who —in a flash of whimsy— called the album an “uncanny masterpiece.” Indeed, it remains a classic. For more see https://eastboston.com/?p=4792

**Paraphrasing a passage from Ralph L. Gleason’s liner notes to Miles Davis’s Bitches Brew. http://albumlinernotes.com/Bitches_Brew.html

Originally posted on January 1, 2022

news_communities.title: Trinitarios member admits to role in deadly Lynn shooting, prosecutors say
news_communities.author: Mike Pescaro
news_communities.summary:
A gang member pleaded guilty to a racketeering charge Friday, admitting to participating in a shooting that left two men dead in Lynn, Massachusetts, according to federal prosecutors.

The shooting on Essex Street on Sept. 2, 2023, killed 21-year-old Jandriel Heredia and 25-year-old Abraham Diaz. Five other people were injured.

The office of Massachusetts U.S. Attorney Leah Foley said Friday that 27-year-old Kelvin Liranzo Roman, also known as Whoopty, had pleaded guilty to conspiracy to conduct enterprise affairs through a pattern of racketeering activity. The charge is for a violation of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organization Act and is commonly referred to as “RICO conspiracy.”

Liranzo Roman is one of 22 alleged Trinitarios members in Massachusetts to be federally charged in February of 2025.

Prosecutors said that Liranzo Roman admitted to being a member of the Trinitarios and being an accessory before the fact in the shooting that killed Heredia and Diaz.

Foley’s office said in a press release that three gang members drove by “a party celebrating a recent high-school graduation and a young man heading off to college,” opening fire and hitting seven people, including the two men who died.

The Essex County District Attorney’s Office brought murder charges against six people in the case the year after the shooting. Prosecutors said 25-year-old Justin Alba of Peabody and five Lynn residents — 20-year-old Darwin Batista, 22-year-old Yefferson Vallecillo Cambar, 21-year-old Abel Severino Reyes, 16-year-old Carlos Ramirez Corniel and 15-year-old Leonardo Espinoza — were indicted in September of 2024.

Four of those people — Alba, Batista, Vallecillo Cambar and Severino Reyes — were among those named by federal prosecutors after the 2025 operation. Two unnamed juveniles, who were 15 and 16 at the time, were also on the list provided by Foley’s office last year.

RICO charges were announced in June against an additional 26 alleged Trinitarios members.

Foley’s office said Liranzo Roman is the 12th person to plead guilty in the operation.

He is scheduled to be sentenced on Nov. 17. Prosecutors said he faces up to life in prison, five years of supervised release and a fine as high as $250,000. He is also subject to deportation.

news_communities.title: Cars and Cops
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
A car show to help raise money for comfort and therapy dogs for law enforcement provided a Saturday of family fun in the Saugus Middle-High School parking lot

 

By Joanie Allbee

 

Last Saturday was a beautiful day for spectators of all ages to hang out at the Saugus Middle-High School. Kids hurried their paces to the school parking lot, leaving parents trailing behind, just as soon as exciting cars and characters came into view at the 7th Annual “Cars and Cops” Car Show. Batman, Bat Girl, The Joker, a Hulk Hogan actor and Police greeted guests warmly and offered to pose for photos.

“It’s been a blast,” exclaimed Saugus Police Officer Domenic Montano, the founder and president of the “Cars and Cops” Car Show.

“We had awesome cars, police cars, theme and movie cars, muscle cars that all came to help raise money for comfort and therapy dogs for law enforcement. Therapy and comfort working dogs are a valuable asset for community members and first responders and veterans,” Montano said.

“[The comfort and therapy dogs are] truly one of our most overlooked tools we have in our belt and truly something we should have more of. All benefit from therapy and comfort dogs. Thank you for coming out to support our four-legged friends. I will see you at the 8th annual ‘Cars and Cops’ car show,” he said.

Officer Montano credits his “Team” for making it happen. The members include his wife, Deanna Montano, the accountant and gate manager; Nicole Stanley, the fundraiser coordinator; Ronald Mikol, the communications supervisor; Robert Rubchinuk, on-site operations; Eddie Ardolino, photographer and provider of assistance wherever needed; and a whole crew of great, hardworking volunteers who put on a fantastic family fundraiser to help bring those in law enforcement therapy and comfort through canines.

Montano expressed deep gratitude for all who came together to give Saugus a memorable “Cars and Cops“ car show. Lt. Jim Harkins of “Peabody Cops For Kids With Cancer“ and his team cooked up delicious breakfast sandwiches, hot dogs and hamburgers for the hungry crowds.

“Great Car show and Fundraiser cause,” said Kenny McDonough, of Stoneham, who annually enters his 1937 Packard Super 8 exclusive convertible.

“And it’s wonderful for families. And every year this car show gets bigger and bigger,” McDonough said.

Karen and Bob Mercurio accompanied their 1970 Ford Mustang in Calypso Coral, of which Carol fondly said, “We just call it orange cause it’s more of an orange color than coral.”

“This is our favorite car show. We come every year,” Carol said. Bob nodded in agreement, with smiles.

Bob and Carol set their car up as if it were at a carhop drive-in – complete with popcorn, milkshake, French fries, burgers, mustard and relish food props and a drive-in speaker. The Mercurios said they love to provide a refreshing walk down memory lane to the guests. Karen was having fun pretending she was a carhop waitress serving Bob at a drive-in.

Andrew Wilgermein arrived from New York with his 2011 Ford Crown Victoria that was formerly a Westchester County, New York Police Department vehicle. “I enjoy preserving the history of Law Enforcement, history in the car community as well as honoring the members of the Law Enforcement Community who have paid the ultimate sacrifice,” Wilgermein said

Eager ticket holders waved streams of blue tickets and gathered around as Saugus Police Officer Montano announced winners. Faces registered shock over the abundance of prizes. There was over $2,000 worth of generous Raffle prizes.

One winner’s prize was two Boston Red Sox Tickets for the August 18 game against the Arizona Diamondbacks. (The game tickets were donated by Jeff Cicolini.)

One woman whose ticket was called hugged the quilt she had won; truly, it was a perfect match.

Trophies were given out for the most popular cars.

Guy Moley of Mom’s Cancer Fighting Angel’s enjoyed being immersed in cars and friends. “I thought the Cars and Cops car show was a complete success,” Moley said.

“As I was walking around, I was stopped by the car attendees saying what a great show it was. I knew it would be. Domenic and his wife Deanna work very hard to make the show a success. Also, the fact that there were other car shows going on at competing times goes to show the ‘Cars and Cops’ car show is one people look forward to because it’s a well-oiled machine,” Moley said.

Cordial Saugus Police Officers were meshed in the crowds, overseeing safety and assuring a fun family atmosphere and relaxed assurance. Madeline Pratico and Patrick Walsh of the Endicott College Police Department handed out stickers and pens and chatted with guests.

As two o’clock drew near, cars were exiting. It was as if an energetic ball of great togetherness that existed throughout the day was slowly dissipating, leaving behind a parking lot of emptiness yet imparting “Cars and Cops” fans with a day of interacting and spectating at a spectacular, successful fundraising event – with the money going for a great cause.

“The Cars and Cops car show is always a great event in Saugus, and it brings Saugus together; always good to see the Classic cars,” Saugonian Mark Turco said.

news_communities.title: J. Pace & Son Celebrates 60 Years with Di Nonna
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
By Tara Vocino

 

  1. Pace & Son celebrated their 60th anniversary last Friday afternoon with their vendor Di Nonna on hand.

Saugus resident Terri Dello Russo, who has been a customer for decades, said she has never had a bad day coming there. Her husband Jerry’s favorite is the chicken Italiano and the wonderful cashiers. He said Di Nonna’s applesauce tastes like apple pie.

Saugus resident Rita Pelosi has been a customer since 1963. “The quality of the food is outstanding,” Pelosi said. “I like the sandwiches and desserts when I have company.”

Susan Pelosi traveled from San Francisco, California, for their Scali bread. “It’s a great store,” Pelosi said.

  1. Pace & Son owner Angela Pace attributed success to her late husband, Joseph. “He was the hardest worker,” Pace said. “He was unforgettable.”
  2. Pace & Son President Cara Pace said her father founded their North End location in 1966. “He loved feeding people,” Cara Pace said. “We want to keep his dedication going.”

Di Nonna Chief Operating Officer Joseph Angelo helped to hand out their famous applesauce with cinnamon. “We’ve been a vendor for three years,” Angelo said. “It’s been a fantastic business partnership.”

Di Nonna Chief Executive Officer Rosemary Saggesse said they were the first to make applesauce with cranberries and San Marzano cocktail sauce. The Saugus company has been in operation for five years.

Angelo said J. Pace is clearly an icon in Saugus, and that Joseph Pace was one of the kindest, hardest working people that he’s ever met.

Saugus resident David Savoie said he has always loved J. Pace. His favorite dish to purchase is salmon, cod, swordfish — and for subs — chicken parmesan, cheesesteak and chicken Italiano. “I’ve been coming here for years,” Savoie said.

Customer Linda Russo said she’d never thought of such a combination — ice cream with cinnamon apple sauce.

news_communities.title: Saugus Gardens in the Summer
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Here’s what’s blooming in town this week to make your walks more enjoyable

 

By Laura Eisener

 

Among the most long-lasting flowering perennials are the tickseeds, members of the composite family (Asteraceae). While the name tickseed may conjure up unappealing images, this plant does not have anything to do with actual ticks except that someone thought the seed was somewhat shaped like either a tick or bedbug and the name stuck. While some of the tickseed species come from South and Central America, most of the ones we find available here originated in North America, mostly central U.S. A few have wild ranges up into Canada. Tickseeds have become very popular with breeders in recent years, leading to new hybrids and named varieties. These are great plants for sunny locations, but don’t tend to bloom as well in shade.

A big selling point of tickseeds in general is that most varieties bloom for several months of the summer. If the faded flowers are removed, they often bloom from June until October in our climate. New flower heads are produced very quickly, so that they may need deadheading every few days. While this is not very difficult, often not requiring any tools other than fingernails, it can be time-consuming. I think of it as “fidget maintenance” in that you can just sit next to them and pick or snip off the faded flowers while thinking of other things. It doesn’t seem to matter much if you just snap off the flower head or carefully snip back to just above the top set of leaves. As with other members of the composite family (daisies, sunflowers, etc.), what most people think of as a flower is actually a head of flowers, the “center” having pistils and stamens but no petals, while an outer border contains “ray florets” with a single petal each.

The flower colors can be very variable and include red, pink, white, yellow, orange and combinations of those colors. There are about 80 species in the tickseed (Coreopsis) genus, although there are several species that were recently reclassified in other genera that had been considered part of this genus. One example is threadleaf tickseed (Anacis verticillata, formerly Coreopsis verticillata), which has a scattered range from Quebec to Georgia, and which has long been cultivated in gardens. The award-winning variety ‘Moonbeam’ (Anacis verticillata ‘Moonbeam’) is the best known, with pale yellow flowers, usually growing two feet tall. Another is the cultivar ‘Zagreb’, named for the capital of Croatia, which has bright lemon-yellow flowers on a cloud of bright green airy leaves. As one of the most compact, growing only about a foot tall, ‘Zagreb’ is a great companion for other perennials in the garden, as it can spread out around them, and the flower color goes well with almost any other flower color imaginable. The very narrow leaves in this species give these plants a fine delicate texture in the garden, which can contrast with large blossoms and bolder foliage planted nearby.

A few tickseeds grow wild in Massachusetts, but they are not common. The pink flowering tickseed (Coreopsis rosea) has pastel pink or occasionally white ray florets. Unlike most others in this genus, pink tickseed prefers moist soils and in the wild is often found at edges of swamps or pond margins and is less drought tolerant than most other species. The popular variety ‘American Dream’ has pink ray flowers with lemon yellow disk florets.

Longtime plant breeder Darrell Probst from Hubbardston, Mass., produced the “Big Bang” series of coreopsis in a variety of colors, then introduced the more compact “Li’l Bang” series. Darwin Perennials produced the “UpTick” series, another line of popular tickseeds. These are all widely available in nurseries, and most have combinations of red and yellow in the ray florets.

Large-flowered tickseed (Coreopsis grandiflora) is native to Canada and much of eastern U.S. The flowers are yellow, with the tips of the ray florets somewhat scalloped in shape. They are among the tallest tickseeds also, often two feet tall when in bloom and sometimes up to three feet tall.

Many hybrids have mouse-eared tickseed (Coreopsis auriculata) in their background. The dwarf variety ‘Nana’ is sometimes used as a ground cover.

Because of the nectar and long bloom period, many butterflies, bees and other pollinators are attracted to the various tickseed species. Deer generally do not eat it, but rabbits and groundhogs may sometimes eat it if other more tasty plants are not available. Given the low rain levels of most of this summer, the drought tolerance exhibited by many tickseed species is a definite asset.

news_communities.title: The Sounds of Saugus
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
By Mark E. Vogler

 

Good morning, Saugus

Hope you are making the most of your summer in a safe, healthy and happy way. There are still three full weeks of summer vacation before Saugus kids head back to class for a new school year. That’s three weeks for parents and kids to shop for new clothes and school supplies. That’s three weeks to relax, to read a book or two for pleasure or do something fun.

It’s an odd summer this year where kids will be going back to school in September instead of late August. The first day of classes for students in grades 6 through 12 is Sept. 2. Classes begin for kids in grades 1 through 5 with half days on Sept. 2 and 3. Pre-K and Kindergarten begins on Sept. 3 with half days. Stay tuned.

 

Election alert: Sept. 1 primary coming

Town Clerk Ellen Schena and her staff have about three weeks and four days to complete preparation for the upcoming Sept. 1 primary election. A major order of business is signing up enough election workers – both paid and volunteers.

Every two years, there is a state election that involves a September primary. With school not being in session yet, it becomes more challenging for the Town Clerk to recruit civic-minded Saugus High School juniors and seniors. So a flyer began circulating headlined “CALLING ALL SAUGUS HIGH JUNIORS AND SENIORS,” with the hopes of attracting civic-minded teens who want to help the elections run smoothly this fall: the State Primary (Sept. 1) and the Nov. 3 State General Election.

“Come work for Community Services to fulfill your high school hours OR you can be a Paid $$$$$$ Election Worker,” the flyer stated.

For those Saugus juniors and seniors who are interested in being paid or volunteer election workers, here are the particulars:

  • 16 years old can work part-time shifts (6 to 8 hours)
  • 17 & 18 year olds can work full shifts (8 to 12 hours)
  • The Town Clerk’s Office can accommodate any hours for interested students.

“Great to have on your College Applications/Resumes,” the flyer noted.

Those who are interested should stop by Town Hall or contact the Town Clerk’s Office to apply to work. Ask for Jacey Ruisi, Saugus Election Coordinator, at 781-231-4102 for more details.

A second flyer went out directed at adults who want to work the polls and earn some extra cash. The Town Clerk’s Office is looking to fill specific shifts: all day, or 6 a.m. to 2 p.m., 2 p.m. to 9 p.m. or swing shifts (accommodating hours). For those who are interested in applying for any of those paid positions, please contact the Town Clerk’s Office at 781-231-4102 or 4013.

 

In-Person Early Voting set for Aug. 22

This week, the Town Clerk’s Office also released information for those registered voters who don’t want to wait until Sept. 1 to vote. In-Person Early Voting for the Sept. 1 State Primary Election will begin on Saturday, Aug. 22, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. in the Community Room of the Saugus Public Library at 295 Central St. Voters should enter through the Taylor Street Entrance. This is also the last day to register to vote in the election.

In-Person Early Voting will be held for five additional days, as follows:

  • Monday, August 24, 2026 – 8:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.
  • Tuesday, August 25, 2026 – 8:15 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Wednesday, August 26, 2026 – 8:15 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Thursday, August 27, 2026 – 8:15 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Friday, August 28, 2026 – 8:15 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

 

Saugus United Parish Food Pantry

The Saugus United Parish Food Pantry will be open today (Friday, August 7), from 9:30-11 a.m. at 50 Essex St. in the basement of Cliftondale Congregational Church. The food pantry welcomes all neighbors facing food insecurity on Friday mornings. Volunteers are also welcome. Please call the Food Pantry Office (781-233-2663) or go to the website (cliftondalecc.org) for details.

 

KOC Crafts fair tomorrow

The Saugus Knights of Columbus No. 1829 will host a crafts fair tomorrow (Saturday, Aug. 8) from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. at 57 Appleton St. in Saugus: baked goods, candles, handmade textiles, jewelry, wood carving and much more. Visitors can also enjoy making their own sundaes or enjoy popcorn, hot dogs, hot coffee, donuts and raffles.

 

Children’s Festival at the Iron Works Aug. 12

The Saugus River Watershed Council and the Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site will be collaborating on a night of family fun next Wednesday (Aug. 12), beginning at 6 p.m. at the Iron Works. This year’s Saugus River Picnic & Children’s Festival will be a free family night for kids and will feature games, refreshing snacks, environmental activities, crafts and music.

The event will coincide with the free Summer Concert Series. The Squeezebox Stompers (Cajun, Zydeco, Blues, Folk) are set to perform.

 

This week’s “Shout Outs”

Precinct 6 Town Meeting Member Jeanie Bartolo, the loyal reader who initiated the weekly “Shout Outs” feature for “The Sounds of Saugus” column, offered this one: “This ‘Shout Out’ is for Chris Tarantino, Coach of the Saugus Sachems Track Camp for placing first among the 18 teams competing! Congratulations to Chris and the 64 young Saugus athletes who participated. You are the pride of Saugus!”

Here’s a collective “Shout Out,” taken from the Saugus Firefighters Local 1003 Facebook Page: “On behalf of Lieutenant Damian ‘Jug’ Drella and his family, thank you to everyone who came out to show their unwavering support during his dignified and honorable return home from Brigham and Women’s Hospital. The outpouring of kindness, respect, and solidarity from our fellow firefighters, public safety partners, family, friends, and community meant more than words can express. As Jug continues his courageous battle with occupational cancer, your support serves as a powerful reminder that he is never fighting alone.

“Special thank you to all who were able to join us on Lt. Drella’s honorable return home, and the companies who covered the town so our members could support our brother the way the fire service does.”

Former Saugus Veterans Service Officer SueAnn Cheung resigned last month to become the new director of the Veterans Services’ Office in the Town of Brookline. In an interview this week, she expressed her appreciation to people in the Saugus veterans community: “I want to give thanks to the Saugus Veterans Council. They’re amazing and were very helpful. I loved all of the relationships and contacts I made in Saugus, especially with the American Legion. I loved going to the American Legion breakfasts on Friday mornings and I tried to go every week. The Legion breakfasts are great. No other town is doing that, as far as I know. That’s amazing and great for the community. I’m proud of all of the events I worked on with the veterans – Veterans Day, Wreaths Across America with the DAR, the Memorial Day Parade. State Rep. Donald Wong showed up at all of the events I went to. He showed up at the weekly breakfasts. He really cares about the veterans. As a VSO in Saugus, I enjoyed working with all of the veterans and the veterans organizations.”

 

Want to “Shout Out” a fellow Saugonian?

This is an opportunity for our paper’s readers to single out – in a brief mention – remarkable acts or achievements by Saugus residents or an act of kindness or a nice gesture. Just send an email (mv***@*****st.net) with a mention in the subject line of “An Extra Shout Out.” No more than a paragraph; anything longer might lend itself to a story and/or a photo.

 

Shining Stars of Starlight Cinema

Saugus Community Television reports a successful debut of its Starlight Cinema Movie Night on Tuesday (Aug. 4) at Parcher Field. This was a makeup date for the event that had to be cancelled last week. Saugus residents gathered on the field to enjoy what amounted to a throwback outdoor movie. This year’s featured film was the beloved family adventure “Jumanji” (1995) starring Robin Williams. The movie is about a magical board game that brings jungle dangers to life. This year’s event featured a large LED movie screen, allowing the film to begin before sunset while still providing an outstanding viewing experience for everyone in attendance.

Michelle Madar Fox, the executive director of Saugus Television, offered a collective “shout out” of the sponsors and others contributing to the success of an event that the organizers hope to build on:

“We want to thank all our sponsors and donors, Starlight Cinema would not have been possible without them.

“Platinum Sponsors: Saugus Cultural Council, Richard A. Kowalsky Insurance Agency, Inc., Eccentricity Studio, and Northeastern Fence & Supply Corporation.

“Gold Sponsors: The Rubin House Assisted Living, and Soc’s Ice Cream.

“Silver Sponsors: Lotus Nails Spa, Tax Shop & Financial Center and Rockland Bank.

“Bronze Sponsors and other Donors: 27Str8 Apparel, MCM Nation, The Moulaison Family and Russo Painting.

“We also want to thank all our vendors who provided food for our viewers. Rick Kowalsky and Cliftondale Congregational Church served up nacho chips and cheese, Tiffany’s Tasty Treats had her signature Chocolate chip cookies and other tasty treats, It just so happened to be National Chocolate Chip Cookie Day as well! Soc’s Ice cream was there with their slush and ice cream sandwiches. And Cliftondale Roast Beef and Pizza swooped in to save the day when our last food vendor backed out the day before. They served pizza by the slice, salads and chicken ziti broccoli alfredo!

“I would also like to highlight superstar Maureen Whitcomb! She’s our superhero event coordinator and nothing would have been possible without her!

“Our first ever starlight cinema was amazing and we look forward to hosting another movie night soon!”

Based on preliminary estimates, the organizers consider the event a smashing success. “We counted about 75 raffle tickets which were passed out to every audience member coming through the gate,” Madar Fox said. “Plus at least another 25 or so including the vendors, volunteers and staff. Definitely about 100 or more in total, which is amazing for a first-time event and rain date.”

 

Free Summer concerts series continues

You know it’s truly summer in Saugus when the Wednesday night crowds start to gather at the Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site, where they sing, clap and dance to the music. It’s that time of year again. Another summer of free outdoor concerts over an eight-week period at the Iron Works began on July 1.

This marks the fifth consecutive summer that the Saugus Public Library and the National Park Service are collaborating on a local outdoor event that seems to get more popular every year. The Saugus Cultural Council (a local arm of the Mass Cultural Council, a state agency) is also a key sponsor of the event. The concerts are free and open to the public. The concert series celebrates local musical talents in Essex County and creates opportunities for residents and visitors to engage with the park during evening hours.

Shows begin at 6 p.m. each Wednesday in August. People can bring blankets and chairs, snacks, etc. Don’t forget to bring a friend, too, to enjoy a couple of hours of music outdoors. The events take place on the stage behind the museum building, and spectators can settle down on the upper lawn. It is suitable for all ages. Restrooms are available until nearly 8 p.m. when the concerts conclude. If weather looks bad for any particular Wednesday, concertgoers are urged to check the library website (www.sauguspubliclibrary.org), which will update for cancellations on that day.

This year’s lineup features a combination of new bands and familiar faces. Concerts begin at 6 p.m. on the Big Lawn each Wednesday through August 19. This week’s scheduled headliner (Aug. 5) was The Implications, a band that performs Rock & Country music. Here is the rest of the schedule for the summer concert series:

  • August 12: Squeezebox Stompers (Cajun, Zydeco, Blues, Folk).
  • August 19: Coco Brown & The Invitation (Motown & Soul).

 

Jewelry Making with Mandy Aug. 17

There will be a special jewelry making program in the Brooks Room of the Saugus Public Library on Monday, Aug. 17. Mothers, daughters, grandmothers and friends of all ages are welcome to join Mandy Roberge in making new items or for help repairing your favorite costume jewelry pieces. From necklaces and bracelets to earrings and keychains, this workshop invites kids, teens and adults to explore beads and findings and different types of wire and hemp to create their own unique pieces to take home. Bring a friend and have some fun!

 

Summer Reading time at the library

The 2026 Summer Reading Program at the Saugus Public Library is underway and will last through Friday, Aug. 21. Here’s a summary of the program:

WHO: Kids Pre-K through 6th grade.

WHAT: Kids read the books they love, log their reading and earn prizes! They’ll enjoy reading what they love, free programs, crafts and activities.

WHY: Don’t lose those hard-earned skills! Summer reading plays a vital role in helping reduce the “Summer Slide” – the learning loss experienced between school years – which can leave students significantly behind their peers. The Saugus Public Schools recommend kids read at least 20 minutes every day. We also recommend reading to your child, even as they become an independent reader. Talk about what you’ve read together. Help them find books they like – we can help with that. Make it a fun part of a daily routine they look forward to!

PRIZES: Every reader wins prizes, and books to keep. We’ll also raffle vouchers for ice cream, pizza, roller skating, mini golf, bowling and much more. Grand prize drawings include tickets to Canobie Lake Park and Nova Adventure Park!

HOW: Download the Beanstack App!

If you’ve used Beanstack before, simply register for our 2026 Summer Reading Challenge.

Veterans Day Bricks Program is Back

The Saugus Veterans Council is pleased to reinstate the Brick Program! After our vendor retired last year (thank you, Del from Pavlok, for working with us over the years), we have found another engraver who will be taking our orders for Veterans Day! Proceeds from the brick sales are devoted to the upkeep of Saugus Veterans Park. If you are interested in purchasing a brick, a 4×8″ is $100 (three lines) and an 8×8″ (five lines) is $200. news_communities.title: Another vacancy in Veterans’ Services Office
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Town’s “very promising” VSO leaves to take job in Brookline

 

By Mark E. Vogler

 

For the second time in less than a year, the town seeks to fill the full-time veterans service officer (VSO) position. The town’s most recent VSO, SueAnn Cheung, resigned early last month after a little more than nine months on the job to become director of the Brookline Veterans’ Services Office.

Cheung told The Saugus Advocate this week that she left the Saugus post for a job with more opportunity and one that was closer to her home. “As a VSO in Saugus, I enjoyed working with the veterans community,” Cheung said.

“And I especially loved working with the Saugus Veterans Council. The Veterans Council is excellent and does amazing work, and the entire community is lucky to have the Veterans Council, because of everything they do,” she said.

“I’m happy to have met each of the veterans I worked with. I hope I gave them great customer service and helped them with their benefits,” she said.

Cheung, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, made Saugus history last Sept. 26 when Town Manager Scott C. Crabtree announced he had hired her to become the town’s first full-time VSO. “I think she’s going to make a great advocate and continue the things that we think are important [for veterans services],” Crabtree told selectmen several days later.

“I think she’s very promising. I think she brings a lot of experience from working at the Veterans Services Office in Boston and for the state. We’re happy to have her on board,” he said.

But Cheung’s service to Saugus was brief. The town began advertising for the vacancy in the veterans office several weeks ago.

“I was disappointed to hear SueAnn left from serving our Veterans for such a short period of time,” said former Selectman Corinne Riley, who has been active in local veterans’ affairs and serves as public affairs officer of the Saugus Veterans Council.

“I wish her well and I’m sure she will serve the Veterans of Brookline well with her experience. I hope that the position in Saugus is filled in a timely manner, as it is an extremely important position and our Veterans deserve a VSO in place quickly,” Riley said.

Saugus Veterans Council Commander Stephen L. Castinetti said he wasn’t surprised about Cheung’s departure. “She had a chance to get closer to home and have a significant increase in pay,” Castinetti noted. The Town of Brookline has a population of 63,766 – more than twice the size of Saugus, which is slightly over 29,000.

Crabtree’s appointment of Cheung last fall was a controversial one in the Saugus veterans community. Then-VSO Paul J. Cancelliere learned he had lost his 18-an-hour-a-week part-time job on June 30, 2025 – the end of the 2025 Fiscal Year. Cancelliere, who had worked in the position for about two years, applied for the full-time VSO position that the town began advertising for in July of last year. But Cancelliere never received an invitation to be interviewed. Meanwhile, the VSO position remained vacant for nearly three months, prompting local veterans to worry about their benefits being jeopardized.

Then in mid-September, several leaders and members of the Saugus Veterans Council took a vocal stand at a Board of Selectmen’s meeting, calling for former Veterans Service Officer Cancelliere to be reappointed full-time to the job he held on a part-time basis for two years. More than three dozen local veterans and members of the Saugus Veterans Council responded in the show of support for Cancelliere – including former Saugus VSO Jay Pinette, who served the town for four years.

“I have heard nothing but glowing praise for the job that Paul has done since he’s been here,” Pinette told selectmen. “And it will be a credit to him and to the town and the veterans and their dependents in Saugus if he is fortunate enough to be reappointed.”

The elimination of Cancelliere’s part-time position happened because of the collapse of the Regional Veterans Service District, which also included Melrose and Wakefield. Under the previous arrangement, Cancelliere was hired by the City of Melrose to work in Saugus. The City of Wakefield previously pulled out of the district.

Castinetti, a former selectman who had been commander of the Saugus Veterans Council for 15 years, told selectmen at their meeting last September that Saugus “had a great VSO until the coalition broke up between Saugus, Melrose and Wakefield” earlier last year. Melrose and Wakefield went on to hire full-time VSOs while Saugus did nothing, Castinetti noted.

“We don’t understand why Paul Cancelliere wasn’t reappointed the day they broke up. Paul has been one of the best VSOs,” Castinetti said.

But less than two weeks later, Crabtree decided that Cheung was the best candidate for the job among those who had applied. “SueAnn brings an exceptional blend of service, leadership, and compassion to the Veterans’ Services Office,” Crabtree said in a press release issued by his office last Sept. 26.

“Her distinguished military background, combined with her extensive work supporting veterans and managing human services programs, make her uniquely qualified to serve as our full-time Veterans’ Service Officer. We are proud to welcome her to this vital role, and we are confident she will have a positive impact on the lives of Saugus veterans and their families,” the town manager said.

In an interview this week, Castinetti said Cancelliere should be the next full-time VSO. “Since there is a vacancy now, I’m hoping Paul Cancelliere applies for it because he should still be the Veterans Service Officer today,” Castinetti said.

“There’s no reason for him to have been replaced by the town manager. There’s no reason for him to not have been picked for a position he had done part-time for over two years,” Castinetti said.

No matter who the town manager hires to be the next VSO, Pinette said, he hopes that filling the position with a qualified candidate as soon as possible is a top priority. “It’s very important that we maintain continuity in delivering Chapter 115 benefits to our neediest veterans and their dependents,” Pinette said.

“The role of the VSO has expanded greatly over the last few years on the VA benefits front. State and Federal funds that are returned to the town as a result of the VSO’s actions make a tremendous difference in the community,” he said.

 

What the job entails

The candidate hired by the town manager to be the next VSO will receive a salary of $75,000 to $85,000 annually, according to the job posting. Their chief responsibilities will be to:

  • Administer the Chapter 115 benefits program for eligible Saugus veterans and their dependents, including processing applications, auditing payments, and generating reports.
  • Assist veterans in applying for federal and state benefits, such as disability, pensions, Aid and Attendance, VA health-care programs, and DD 214 upgrades.
  • Serve as the Town’s primary resource for veterans’ services, connecting veterans and their families with counseling, health care, housing assistance and social service programs; will also help families with burial benefits and grave markers.
  • Collaborate with other Town departments and community partners to maintain veterans’ memorials and organize events and outreach initiatives.
  • Represent the Veterans’ Services Office at Veterans Advisory Board meetings, coordinate budgets for the department, and work closely with the Executive Office of Veterans Services (EOVS) and regional VSOs.
  • Maintain the confidentiality of veterans’ records, manage departmental staff and projects and participate in continuing education and accreditation.

Residents seeking assistance or information about veterans’ benefits and programs are encouraged to contact the Saugus Veterans’ Services Office at 781-231-4010 or visit www.saugus-ma.gov/veterans-services-office. The Saugus Veterans’ Service Office is also staffed by Nancy Stead, the Veterans’ Services Office Administrative Assistant, who can be reached at 781-231-4196.

news_communities.title: Man found dead in Lynn, prompting police investigation
news_communities.author: Marc Fortier and Asher Klein
news_communities.summary:
A man was found dead Thursday morning in Lynn, Massachusetts, officials say, and the circumstances around it were under investigation.

The body was reported about 6:18 a.m. on South Common Street, the Essex County District Attorney’s Office said. The identity of the man and how he died were being investigated by state and local police, as well as the state’s medical examiner’s office.

Prosecutors and Lynn police said in an update Friday that the man’s death was an apparent case of homicide, with no indication of a wider threat to the public. Few details were released, and the man was only identified as being 52 and having apparent trauma.

Earlier, Lynn police said they had units for “an active investigation.” The scene is near Market Square.

Aerial video showed several police vehicles and about a dozen officers outside of a multi-unit building. Yellow police tape was cordoning off the area.

news_communities.title: Developers Look to New Plan for Revere Beach Parkway Project
news_communities.author: Record Staff
news_communities.summary:
By Adam Swift

The development team behind a proposed project at the former Russo Tux and Limo at 320 Revere Beach Parkway has withdrawn its plans for a 67-unit residential building.

The proposed six-floor building project initially came before the planning and zoning boards this spring. While the development did garner support from several city councilors, there were concerns raised by board members and abutters about the size of the project.

Anthony Rossi, the project attorney, initially said the developers would take the feedback and come back to the planning and zoning boards with a revised proposal.

Last week, the planning board unanimously approved the developer’s request to withdraw the application for the project without prejudice. The move gives the developers more time to bring a revised plan for the property back to the city.

“They are submitting revised plans, and it just makes sense for them to withdraw fully and reapply with new plans, especially since this plan has been continued over the past couple of months,” said Permitting and Land Use Planning Director Will Cecio. “It allows for re-advertising, and more public notices with more accurate information on what plans they are providing.”

In other business at last week’s meeting, the planning board recommended approvals for special permits and variances for two smaller building projects.

Both projects earned the praise of several board members who noted they were responsible projects that would add housing to the city stock.

The first recommendation for approval was for Christopher Friend at 37 and 37R Central Ave. Friend is looking to build an addition on the second and third floor of an existing residence and expand it from a three- to a four-family home.

The second approval was for the separation of a lot at 1 Lafayette Ave., allowing for the construction of a new two-family home, while keeping the existing two-family home on the property.

Both projects will be before the zoning board of appeals at its regular meeting on Tuesday, August 11 for a potential final vote on the needed special permits and variances.

news_communities.title: Markey, Pressley Release Report Showing Success of Fare-free Transit
news_communities.author: Record Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Record

Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), member of the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, and Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) released a new report, Making Transit Free, Frequent, and Reliable: Massachusetts shows the need for federal investment in fare-free transit, detailing the need for increased federal investments in fare-free transit. Senator Markey and Congresswoman Pressley are lead sponsors of the Freedom to Move Act, which would provide $25 billion to communities to pilot fare free service and expand existing transit service.

news_communities.title: Maltez presents Key to the City to MCU President and CEO Robert Cashman
news_communities.author: Record Staff
news_communities.summary:
Metro honored for its 100th anniversary

By Cary Shuman

City Manager Fidel Maltez presented the Key to the City – Chelsea’s highest honor – to Metro Credit Union President and CEO Robert Cashman during an impressive ceremony at its main headquarters on Revere Beach Parkway.

Maltez made the special visit to celebrate the extraordinary milestone of Metro Credit Union’s 100th anniversary. He also presented a congratulatory citation from the Chelsea City Council.

“I’m here today to honor Metro Credit Union and wish you another 100,” said Maltez. “It’s pretty incredible the history you’ve had, the expansion you’ve had, the success that you’ve had, and it’s so special that the story began in Chelsea. Thank you for everything you do.”

“And this is the official Key to the City that gets you into every building in Chelsea,” jested Maltez.

Cashman humbly accepted the award, stating, “Thank you very much. Metro Credit Union has been a longstanding partner of the city. We couldn’t have done this, with all the success that we’ve had currently without our partners, and obviously the City of Chelsea has been a strong partnership, and we’re very excited about continuing that on. And thank you for all you’ve done to make Chelsea what it is.”

Metro Credit Union was founded in 1926 with the guiding principle of “People Helping People.” Since then, Metro has grown into the largest state-chartered credit union in Massachusetts with more than 220,000 members.

news_communities.title: Governor Healey Lays out Energy Affordability Priorities
news_communities.author: Record Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

Governor Maura Healey called for swift action and passage of her energy affordability legislation to lower energy bills and rein in utility spending. In a letter to members of the conference committee negotiating the final bill, the Governor demanded the utilities stop fighting customer refunds and urged lawmakers to move quickly after their initial meeting to deliver relief for Massachusetts households and businesses by changing how utilities do business, getting charges off bills, and building more local sources of energy.

“It is absolutely outrageous that, at a time when the people of Massachusetts are struggling to pay their energy bills, utility spending, profits and shareholder payouts are skyrocketing,” said Governor Healey. “Enough is enough. Massachusetts ratepayers shouldn’t be footing the bill for unnecessary utility spending or excessive profits. And they shouldn’t be locked into paying high energy costs driven by President Trump’s Iran war. Passing my energy affordability legislation will ensure ratepayers are getting the best deal for energy, eliminate unnecessary charges from people’s bills, rein in utility spending and profits, and lower costs. Utilities also need to drop their legal challenges to our efforts to return money to consumers and stop seeking rate hikes that people simply can’t afford.”

“Our energy affordability legislation meets the moment we are in. We need to act as Trump’s war drives up energy prices worldwide and utility infrastructure spending raises ratepayer bills,” said Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper. “Our administration is ready to act to implement this critical legislation. We’re ready to strike charges, procure more energy, and increase oversight over utility spending.”

Since Governor Healey filed her energy affordability legislation in May 2025, Massachusetts gas and electric utilities have continued seeking higher profits, increasing shareholder payouts, opposing efforts to rein in spending, and pursuing additional rate increases.

As profits have risen, National Grid, Eversource, Berkshire Gas and Liberty Gas have all sought rate increases in the past year, some as high as 55 percent, driven in part by significant infrastructure spending that also increases utility profits. Governor Healey has opposed those increases, and her administration has consistently argued before the Department of Public Utilities for stronger oversight and lower utility profit levels.

The utilities, which also earn profits from other arms of their businesses like transmission investments, have fought efforts to return exorbitant profit back to ratepayers. Earlier this year, FERC ordered the New England transmission owners to return approximately $1.5 billion in profits collected over the past decade after advocacy by then-AG Healey and current AG Campbell. FERC also cut the allowed return on equity going forward. The transmission owners appealed this ruling, called for a slower rollout of the refund, and doubled down on increasing transmission profits going forward. Governor Healey and AG Campbell opposed this proposal and rallied all New England Governors to oppose the proposal. 

Meanwhile, shareholder payouts keep going up. Last year, Eversource and National Grid shareholders received billions in direct payouts.

Governor Healey’s energy affordability legislation gives the state new tools to lower energy bills by bringing more affordable energy online, reducing unnecessary costs for customers, and holding utilities accountable for excessive spending and profits. In her letter to the conference committee, she highlights key provisions that should remain in the bill to reduce costs, strengthen oversight and help deliver more affordable, reliable energy across Massachusetts. This includes changing how energy is purchased to get the best deals, eliminating fees and profit adders paid to utilities, getting charges off bills, avoiding unnecessary utility spending, bringing more energy into Massachusetts faster and more affordably and allowing the DPU to initiate audits of the utilities.  Governor Healey also urged the committee to include protections for ratepayers, communities and the environment from higher costs and other negative impacts driven by data centers, in keeping with her recently released framework.

news_communities.title: The Amp at Suffolk Downs to host Beatles tribute concert celebrating 60 years since band’s famous on-site performance
news_communities.author: Special to the Independent
news_communities.summary:
This Friday, Suffolk Downs will commemorate the 60th anniversary of The Beatles’ legendary 1966 Suffolk Downs concert with a free tribute concert by 4EverFab at The Amp, the site’s new 600-person outdoor amphitheater.

In celebration of the 60-year anniversary of The Beatles’ legendary August 1966 concert at Suffolk Downs, The HYM Investment Group is excited to host the 4EverFab Beatles Band for a free tribute concert at The Amp, plus local food trucks, beer from on-site brewery Twisted Fate Brewing, and family-friendly activities, Friday, August 7 from 6 to 9 p.m. 

The Amp at Suffolk Downs located at 125 Salt Street, Revere, MA 02151

All are welcome to attend, free ticket reservation encouraged. 

In 2017, Suffolk Downs, located in both East Boston and Revere along two MBTA Blue Line Stops, was purchased by HYM and its investors with a vision to create a welcoming neighborhood designed around new ways of living and working. Today, the 161-acre site at Suffolk Downs is being reborn as a new urban district with a dynamic mix of uses and offerings connected and supported by public open space, neighborhood retail, and civic spaces. Suffolk Downs will deliver 5.2M SF of life science and office space, 10.15M SF of residential space, 450K SF of retail space, 400K SF of hotel space and over 40 acres of open space. Phase 1 of the redevelopment broke ground in May 2022 on the Revere side of the site and the first building, Amaya, delivered in 2024. The second multifamily building at Suffolk Downs, Portico, officially broke ground in 2025 and will deliver 473 units of housing to the Revere community upon completion.

news_communities.title: New England Aquarium applauds Boston flood protection plan
news_communities.author: Special to the Times-Free Press
news_communities.summary:
Given its location on Boston’s waterfront, the New England Aquarium is particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, experiencing flooding during storm surges, king tides, and other extreme weather. Since 2019, the Aquarium has been among those leading the conversation about sea level rise and the importance of coastal preparedness, advocating for a comprehensive resiliency plan for Boston and championing a downtown waterfront for all—one that is resilient, accessible, and inclusive. The Aquarium is a member of A Better City, Boston Waterfront Partners, the Coalition for a Resilient and Inclusive Waterfront (founding partner), the Green Ribbon Commission, and the Wharf District Council—all entities invested in advancing this vision. For the last two years, the Aquarium has engaged with the City of Boston and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) as they conducted the Coastal Storm Risk Management Study for the City of Boston.

In response to the release of the full Draft Integrated Feasibility Report and Programmatic Environmental Assessment, the New England Aquarium is sharing the below statement from President and CEO Vikki N. Spruill.

“The New England Aquarium applauds the City of Boston and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, whose Draft Integrated Feasibility Report would protect lives and billions of dollars in public and private assets along the waterfront and inland from future coastal flood events and sea level rise, while paving the way for an accessible, resilient, and inclusive waterfront for all. The proposed comprehensive system plan is a necessary and wise investment in Boston’s future, created through a process that provides a pathway to federal investment. Now, Boston has the ability and the opportunity to demonstrate what is possible when public leadership, private investment, scientific expertise, and civic ambition come together around the common goal of making our great city a global model for coastal resilience.”

The New England Aquarium is a nonprofit research and conservation organization that has protected and cared for our ocean and marine animals for more than 55 years. We provide science-based solutions and help shape policies that create measurable change to address threats the ocean faces. We inspire action through discovery and help create engaged, resilient communities.

news_communities.title: Helping rescue animals
news_communities.author: Penny & Ed Cherubino
news_communities.summary:
There are many ways you can help dogs in rescue situations. You could volunteer with a rescue group or shelter and see what assignments might fit your lifestyle and schedule. You could walk dogs and play with cats, giving critters one-on-one attention while they are in the shelter. If you have more time, you could visit and assess potential adoptive homes. You could also help transport animals to and from shelters, foster homes, or new families.

Foster Homes

If you’ve ever wondered whether there’s room in your life for another dog or cat, you might try fostering an animal. This is simply providing shelter, training, comfort, and affection to an animal in your home for a few weeks. Your assessment of the animal can be used to match them with a permanent home that will suit their personality, activity level, and behavior.

Fostering depends on your own animals as well as the rescue. Our second Westie, Maggie Mae, was a social butterfly who loved spending time with other dogs. We fostered dogs until she reached her senior years and needed more of our attention. You also have to be sure the incoming dog has been cleared as free of any issues that might harm your family, including children and animals.

One of our mentors in Westie Rescue used to say, “All rescues come with baggage. We have to help them unpack.” This has always been the approach we’ve taken with the dogs we fostered, and we passed on this advice as we delivered dogs to their new homes.

Home Visits

Home visits fit into our current lifestyle. With each request, we can choose to take on the task or not. Since we don’t have a car, we often visit homes accessible by MBTA. Our understanding of city life helps us prepare a report that is fair to the rescue group and the prospective family.

Home visit volunteers are the eyes and ears of the people who process applications and make the decisions about placing dogs in what they call “forever” homes.

We also answer questions about the breed, and warn of possible dangers around the house that someone who has not lived with a tenacious terrier might not spot.

Transporting

Many rescue groups move dogs long distances with volunteer drivers. We’ve driven some of these runs and helped coordinate a Westie transport group for many years. A route is planned from the foster home that has the dog to where the pup can be handed over to the adoptive family. Coordinating transport is the type of job that can be done by any reliable person from their home.

There are also opportunities to transport by air if you are traveling between cities and would be willing to take a small dog in the cabin with you. We’ve been the local connection for volunteers flying into Logan.

Leaders & Worker Bees

Every rescue group needs leadership and worker bees. People make phone calls to shelters, pick up dogs at homes where they are being surrendered, take the dogs in rescue to veterinary visits, nurse them after surgery or as they recover from neglect, injury, or illness.

Finally, you can provide financial support. From writing a check to devoting your life, there is a place for you if you’d like to do your bit to help homeless animals. Pick a group, pick a task, and give it a try. Each success along the way will fill your heart with joy.

news_communities.title: City of Everett celebrates Nepal Day with GBNC
news_communities.author: Special to the Independent
news_communities.summary:
The City of Everett joined the Greater Boston Nepali Community (GBNC) in celebrating Nepal Day, welcoming residents and visitors to Glendale Park for an afternoon of culture, music, food, and community.

On Sunday, August 2, hundreds gathered at Glendale Park where local vendors filled the baseball field with authentic Nepali cuisine, including Dal Bhat Tarkari, Momos, and Sel Roti. Throughout the afternoon, attendees enjoyed traditional music, cultural performances, and Nepali dance, creating a vibrant celebration of one of Everett’s many diverse communities.

“Everett is proud to be home to so many cultures and traditions, and Nepal Day is a wonderful example of what makes our community unique,” said Mayor Robert J. Van Campen. “It’s always inspiring to see so many people come together to celebrate, learn from one another, and enjoy a day that reflects the diversity of our city.”

Founded in 1989, the Greater Boston Nepali Community is a thriving association of Nepalis and friends of Nepal living throughout the greater Boston area. Today, the organization includes more than 600 students, professionals, and families.

“On behalf of the GBNC, I would like to express our heartfelt gratitude to the City of Everett for partnering with us in celebrating Nepal Day 2026 for the fourth consecutive year,” said Sandip Bhattarai, President of the Greater Boston Nepali Community. “This event is a wonderful opportunity to share Nepal’s rich culture, traditions, music, dance, and cuisine while bringing together people from all backgrounds in the spirit of unity and inclusion. We sincerely thank Mayor Robert Van Campen, the City Council, city officials, volunteers, sponsors, and our community partners for their continued support. Their commitment to celebrating diversity has helped make Nepal Day a meaningful and successful community tradition. We look forward to continuing this valued partnership for many years to come.”

Nepal Day is one of many cultural celebrations held throughout Everett each year, reflecting the City’s commitment to embracing its diverse communities and creating opportunities for residents to learn from and celebrate one another.

news_communities.title: Crimson Tide Youth Football draws huge turnout for 2026 season
news_communities.author: Cary Shuman
news_communities.summary:
Crimson Tide Youth Football pre-season practices have begun, and the turnout is impressive.

Nick Olson, beginning his second year as president following the organization’s move from Pop Warner to American Youth Football (AYF) in 2025, reports that more than 300 athletes (football players and cheerleaders) are enrolled in the program.

“We started our year with practices at Everett Stadium last week, and this week we’re at Sacramone Park,” said Olson, a former Everett High football player who served in the United States Marine Corps. “We’re encouraged by the large influx of new players. We have double the number of cheerleaders and we have 35 additional football players. We’re going to have well over 300 participants this year (ages 6-14).”

The 14U cheer team, led by coach Deanna Massa, is the defending state champion and finished in the top five at Nationals in Kissimmee, Florida, Olson noted proudly. The 8U football team was a New England finalist.

The football teams will wear uniforms matching the San Francisco 49ers colors (scarlet and gold) worn by the Everett High football team. “We made sure we put the ‘E’ stickers on the helmets. We look identical to Everett High School,” said Olson.

Leo, Cafarella return as coaches

Olson announced that legendary coaches Chuck Leo and Frank Cafarella have returned to the program and will lead the Everett 8U football team. One of the players is Leo’s grandson, Mance McKinney.

Leo brings more than 45 years of football coaching to the program, with several league, state, and regional titles, and appearances in the nationals on his awe-inspiring resume.

“We’re happy to have these two outstanding coaches back and helping our program,” said Olson.

Olson said Everett High head football coach Rob DiLoreto has been very helpful to the Crimson Tide Youth Football organization.

“Rob has been very engaged with our program,” said Olson. “Any time we’ve called on Rob for his insight or guidance, he’s stepped up and opened the dialogue between Everett High and Everett youth football.”

Olson is being assisted on the executive board by vice president Julie Carapellucci, treasurer Diana Groux, secretary Ashley Franklin, football director LeRoy Heard, and cheer director Sheena DeSalvo.

Everett will open its regular season against Dorchester on Sunday, Aug. 30 at Everett Stadium.

news_communities.title: Signs of summer’s end
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Signs of summer’s end

All in all, this has been a pretty good summer. The weather has been as close to perfect as we could expect for summer activities. The mornings along our coastline have been pleasantly placid for those of us who row on the ocean — we belong to a rowing club on the South Shore that ventures up and down the coast and as far out as Minots Light — while the breezes typically have been picking up in the afternoon for the sailors.

Our vegetable and flower gardens — which are entirely contained in large pots on the patio of our condo — once again have been superb. We’ve had more tomatoes than we know what to do — and nothing beats the pop in our mouths of freshly-picked tomatoes in the summer (as opposed to those tasteless tomatoes that we have to settle for in grocery stores in the winter months).

However, all good things must come to an end, and so too it is with summer. The days now are noticeably shorter. With the sunset inching southward each day, the shadows cast in the late afternoon and early evening are far different than they were in June and July.

The blooming purple loosestrife — though it is an invasive species, we have to admit it is quite striking with its spiky purple flowers — is another harbinger that we have reached the back nine of summer. So too, are the tips of the marsh grass; a few weeks ago they were a verdant green, but now they are turning a golden yellow, yet another indication of the inevitable downward trajectory of the summer of 2026.

With parents and children gearing up for the start of the 2026-27 school year in just a few weeks, yet another summer season is sadly winding down.

Our long-time publisher, Andrew P. Quigley, who lived an extraordinary life, used to say, “When you look back on your life, you realize that all you really have are your memories.”

What summertime means to us — whether it be the time we spend with our families and friends or long walks by ourselves on a summer evening — reinforces the notion that the best things in life are free.

It also is a truism that while life itself is short, summer seems to pass in the blink of an eye. All of us will be saying both to ourselves and to each other on the Tuesday after Labor Day: “Where did the summer go?”

So let’s make the most of what is left of the summer of 2026. It never is too late to make memories that will last a lifetime.

news_communities.title: Harlem Lacrosse introduces the sport to hundreds of Boston kids
news_communities.author: Malcolm Johnson
news_communities.summary:
For University of Mount Saint Vincent lacrosse player Naveah Martin, picking up a lacrosse stick changed the course of her life.

“When I first started playing lacrosse in middle school, I wasn’t really doing anything productive,” Martin said. “Harlem Lacrosse gave me something to do in the afternoons and allowed me to be with my friends. Then we started going to bigger cities and I began meeting new people.”

Martin is one of many former participants who credit Harlem Lacrosse with opening doors on and off the field.

The nonprofit organization, which combines year-round lacrosse programming with academic support, leadership development and mentorship, hosted a free summer clinic Tuesday for more than 300 children in Boston, many of whom were playing the sport for the first time.

Babson College lacrosse player Daivyon Williams also discovered the game through Harlem Lacrosse.

“The first time I touched a stick was in sixth grade and I fell in love with it,” Williams said.

Williams originally hoped to play football but found a different opportunity through lacrosse.

“I wanted to play football and I wasn’t good enough,” he said. “But as soon as I played lacrosse, it was different, and I knew it would be on a different path, but I could excel in it.”

Harlem Lacrosse Boston Executive Director Patrick Cronan said introducing young people to the sport is about more than learning the game.

“Coming out here, you can just tell with the amount of smiles everywhere you look,” Cronan said. “Even the kids that were a little bit defensive and had their guard up and might’ve been too cool to try something new — everyone’s smiling and having a good time. There is something there for everyone.”

The organization was founded about 15 years ago by Massachusetts state Rep. Simon Cataldo, who was teaching special education in Harlem at the time.

“None of my students had played an organized sport before,” Cataldo said. “We went down with a whistle and a clipboard. About 15 years later, this thing is happening all across the country now.”

Cataldo said the organization’s impact extends well beyond athletics.

“Our students are now earning well over $150 million in academic scholarships,” he said. “Our kids are in Ivy League schools and community colleges.”

Massachusetts state Rep. Christopher Worrell, who partnered with Harlem Lacrosse to host Tuesday’s clinic, said exposing children to new activities is especially important.

“Making sure our kids have access to something new and getting them outside of the house is important,” Worrell said. “Every year we try to make sure kids enjoy themselves and experience something they’ve never played before. You hear the laughter — it was amazing.”

Organizers hope the clinic inspires the next generation of players, just as it did for Martin and Williams, whose first experiences with the sport eventually led them to compete at the collegiate level.
